lesson.title: Sealed and Under Pressure: Inside the Bomb Calorimeter
lesson.summary: A bomb calorimeter is a heavy, sealed steel vessel used to measure the heat released by combustion reactions at constant volume, which means it measures the change in internal energy rather than enthalpy directly.
lesson.body:
Some reactions, especially combustion, release far too much energy and require far too much oxygen gas to run safely inside a foam cup. For these reactions chemists use a bomb calorimeter: a thick walled, rigid steel vessel (the bomb) that holds the sample and an excess of oxygen gas at high pressure, sealed shut, and submerged in a known mass of water inside an insulated outer container. The sample is ignited electrically, combustion occurs completely within the sealed bomb, and the heat released warms the bomb, the surrounding water, and the whole calorimeter assembly, which is monitored with a precise thermometer.

This design is built to approximate an isolated system rather than merely a closed one. The steel bomb keeps every gas molecule produced by the reaction trapped inside, so no matter escapes, and the whole assembly is heavily insulated from the outside lab, so essentially no heat escapes either. That is precisely why bomb calorimeters achieve such high precision. All of the energy released by the reaction stays within the boundaries of the calorimeter, where it can be fully accounted for by the temperature rise of the water bath.

The defining physical feature of a bomb calorimeter is that its volume never changes. The steel vessel is rigid, so delta V = 0. Since expansion work is defined as w = negative P delta V, a fixed volume means the reaction does zero work on its surroundings. With no work term to worry about, the first law of thermodynamics reduces to the statement that all of the heat measured, called q at constant volume or q(v), equals exactly the change in internal energy of the system, q(v) = delta U. This is different from a coffee cup calorimeter, which, at constant pressure, measures enthalpy change instead. A bomb calorimeter simply cannot hand you delta H directly. It hands you delta U.

Because a real bomb calorimeter includes not just water but also the steel bomb, wires, and thermometer, chemists rarely calculate its heat capacity from scratch. Instead the whole assembly is calibrated ahead of time by burning a reference substance with a precisely known energy content and measuring the resulting temperature change, which yields a single combined heat capacity, C(calorimeter), exactly the extensive quantity you met in the heat capacity chapter, just applied to the entire device rather than one substance. Once C(calorimeter) is known, the heat released by any later combustion is simply q = C(calorimeter) times delta T.

For example, a 1.500 g sample of fuel is burned completely inside a bomb calorimeter whose total heat capacity, from calibration, is 8.20 kJ/degree C. The temperature of the water bath rises from 24.00 degrees C to 26.44 degrees C, so delta T = 2.44 degrees C. The heat released is q = C(calorimeter) times delta T = (8.20 kJ/degree C)(2.44 degrees C) = 20.0 kJ. Since the reaction released this heat, and the measurement was made at constant volume, delta U(combustion) = negative 20.0 kJ for this 1.500 g sample. Notice this value is delta U, not delta H. For many reactions the two are numerically close, but they are not identical, and the exact size of that gap depends on how many moles of gas the reaction consumes or produces, a detail you will work through quantitatively when you reach enthalpy of combustion.
